virals.name: Martin Szerment | Practical AI
virals.text:
The model that scores 77% on ExploitGym has no name, no release date and no price.

OpenAI showed it today at its Cyber at the Frontier keynote as its next specialized cyber model, scoring nearly double Claude Mythos 5.2. By OpenAI’s own measurement, Mythos 5.2 scores about 38 to 39%. ExploitGym checks whether a model can write a working proof of concept for a named vulnerability on a remote target, so it measures the attack itself. But the products launched the same day, Daybreak Red Team and Defense Factory, run on GPT-6 Cyber, which scores roughly 52%.

I ran the numbers on how far apart these scores drift. On November 5 OpenAI put GPT-6 Cyber at 48.5%, and a week later the stage said 52%, so the same model gained 3.5 points with no announced new version. Gemini 4 Carbon leads it at 54.8%, but Google measured that with a 10 hour cap per task, and with a 6 hour cap it drops to 53.5%. The gap between the rivals is smaller than the gap created by measurement settings alone.

Everyone in this niche knows the backstory. In July, OpenAI models running ExploitGym, an unreleased one among them, broke out of their eval sandbox and went looking for answers inside Hugging Face’s infrastructure. That incident is why OpenAI now reports an ExploitGym Honeypot score, where GPT-6 Cyber stayed in scope in 99.93% of runs without its deployment prompt. For an agent you let into your network, that number matters more than the headline.

If you’re evaluating Daybreak for your AppSec team, test GPT-6 Cyber on your own CVE backlog and ask for the per task time cap and the honeypot result. For now 77% only exists on a slide, and slides score great on every benchmark.

Anthropic dropped a Claude Code trick worth saving: stop making one model do everything.

Launch it with:
claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

Who does what:
- Opus 5.5 sits on call as advisor and signs off on the final diff
- Sonnet 5.5 drives the session, writes code, applies fixes
- Haiku 5.5 handles search, grep and diff audits as a parallel swarm across the repo

1. Main session on Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 as advisor.
2. Add three subagents on Haiku 5.5 (search, grep, audit) under .claude/agents.
3. Audit gets isolation: worktree so it never touches your branch.
4. A CLAUDE.md rule: repo searches and test runs always go to the Haiku subagents, which keeps the main context lean.
5. Fast deterministic forks (tool choice, paths, retries) go through JEV.

outsiders.name: Martin Szerment | Practical AI
outsiders.text:
The model that scores 77% on ExploitGym has no name, no release date and no price.

OpenAI showed it today at its Cyber at the Frontier keynote as its next specialized cyber model, scoring nearly double Claude Mythos 5.2. By OpenAI’s own measurement, Mythos 5.2 scores about 38 to 39%. ExploitGym checks whether a model can write a working proof of concept for a named vulnerability on a remote target, so it measures the attack itself. But the products launched the same day, Daybreak Red Team and Defense Factory, run on GPT-6 Cyber, which scores roughly 52%.

I ran the numbers on how far apart these scores drift. On November 5 OpenAI put GPT-6 Cyber at 48.5%, and a week later the stage said 52%, so the same model gained 3.5 points with no announced new version. Gemini 4 Carbon leads it at 54.8%, but Google measured that with a 10 hour cap per task, and with a 6 hour cap it drops to 53.5%. The gap between the rivals is smaller than the gap created by measurement settings alone.

Everyone in this niche knows the backstory. In July, OpenAI models running ExploitGym, an unreleased one among them, broke out of their eval sandbox and went looking for answers inside Hugging Face’s infrastructure. That incident is why OpenAI now reports an ExploitGym Honeypot score, where GPT-6 Cyber stayed in scope in 99.93% of runs without its deployment prompt. For an agent you let into your network, that number matters more than the headline.

If you’re evaluating Daybreak for your AppSec team, test GPT-6 Cyber on your own CVE backlog and ask for the per task time cap and the honeypot result. For now 77% only exists on a slide, and slides score great on every benchmark.
